*************************************************************** ENDF/B-VIII.0 EVAL-Oct16 Brown,Nobre,Herman,Leal,Trkov,+ Original ENDF/B-VIII.0 evaluation from the CIELO project The evaluation, file assembly and criticality validation were performed at BNL and IAEA by D.A. Brown, G.P.A. Nobre, M. Herman, R. Arcilla, L.Leal, R. Capote, A. Trkov
Primary reference: Nucl. Data Sheets 148, 214 (2018) The evaluation was performed up to 150 MeV for 7 subsequent neutron emissions, 3 proton emissions and a single alpha- particle, deuteron, triton, and 3He for a total of 146 residual nuclei. Only 5 of these were treated as exclusive, i.e., had an explicit reaction assigned to them along with the corresponding exclusive spectra for all particles and gammas. The exclusive reactions were (n,g), (n,elas), (n,inel), (n, 2n), (n,p), and (n, 2p). For all the remaining we provide cross sections for residua production which represent a sum of contributions from all possible reactions populating a given residue. Their respective spectra are lumped together providing only seven cumulative spectra (for gammas, neutrons, protons, alphas, deuterons, tritons, and 3He) for all the inclusive channels.
Development of the evaluation is traced in the CIELO-iron project on the NNDC GForge server: https://ndclx4.bnl.gov/gf/project/cielo_iron All elements of the evaluation, such as experimental datasets, EMPIRE inputs and outputs, intermediate ENDF files and plots can be followed there in a chronological order.
EXPERIMENTAL DATABASE -------------------- The experimental database used in the evaluation is summarized in Table IX of the primary reference (NDS 148,241(2018)). In doing this selection we favored: (i) broad energy range covered by the experiment, (ii) high energy resolution, and (iii) high (but reasonable) accuracy of the experiment. Thus the measurements providing possibly wide and reliable picture were given precedence over single energy-point experiments, especially within the energy range where strong fluctuations were observed. On the other hand, many single- or a few-point measurements adopted when no extended datasets were available. Some of the measured datasets were renormalized to account for changes in the reference cross sections since they were used in the analysis of the experiments. The renormalizations built into the EXFOR retrieval system were adopted. In case of the (n,p) and (n,2n) reactions we took advantage of the existing high quality evaluations available from the IRDFF library (INDC(NDS)-0616, IAEA, Vienna (2012)) and used these data instead of the actual measurements.
RESOLVED RESONANCE RANGE ------------------------ MF=2 MT=151 Resolved resonances The evaluation in the resonance region in based on the version of the Atlas that was still in development at the time our work was performed [3]. The compilation in the Atlas appeared to use parameters generated in Reich-Moore approximation. Because the Atlas also contained resonance parameters for resonances in the first (n,n) state, we decided to convert the Atlas compilation to the LRF=7 format using Reich-Moore approximation, including the first inelastic state. The change from MLBW Atlas parameters to LRF=7 parameters necessitated a refitting of the bound levels and R-prime. This change did improve agreement between the evaluation and experiment in the minima between resonances. The capture widths were known only from the area under each resonance. Additionally we added several resonances at the upper end of the RRR to improve agreement of the RRR with data in the region of 140-165 keV. The (n,n) resonances were determined by identifying capture resonances with no elastic counterpart and subtracting the capture width from the total width determined from (n,tot) measurements. The (n,n) resonances were assumed to be s-wave only. This choice was supported by the experimental results of Ref. [1] and Ref. [2]. Our thermal cross section and computed resonance integral values are in excellent agreement with the Atlas recommendations [3], as shown in the table below. Our MACS(30 keV) value lies roughly in between the JENDL-4.0 and KADoNiS-0.3 values and is generally consistent with the experimental averaged value given in the new Atlas. The Atlas value derived from systematics is more consistent with the KADoNiS-0.3 value. We note that the in-development version of KADoNiS-1.0 recommends a value basically taken from the Giubrone thesis [4], measured at CERN n-TOF. This measurement does not span the whole energy range of the resonance region. Therefore Giubrone omits several low energy resonances that would have provided a smooth background to the 30 keV region, lowering the MACS(30 keV) value obtained from the consideration of that set alone. Thus we use the MACS data for validation purposes only.

REACTION MODELING IN FAST NEUTRON RANGE --------------------------------------- The fast region calculations were performed using the EMPIRE code, which is a comprehensive package that integrates into a single system a number of important physical modules and evaluation tools. We have adopted coupled channel (CC) calculations in the incident channel and for the direct inelastic scattering to collective levels. In addition, we have allowed for the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) to populate presumably collective levels which are not included in the ground state band used in the CC calculations to adjust neutron emission spectra in the high energy range. For the preequilibrium (PE) emission employed the classical exciton model (PCROSS module) because of its higher flexibility in modeling neutron spectra compared with the physically more advanced, but also more rigid quantum mechanical models. The same module was also used for the PE emission of protons and gammas as well as for PE emission of clusters, the latter taking advantage of the Iwamoto-Harada model. The Hauser-Feshbach formulation of the statistical model was employed to follow sequential emission of particles from the compound nucleus (CN). The elastic and inelastic angular distributions of neutrons emitted from the CN were calculated using the Blatt-Biedenharn formalism. The width fluctuation factor was accounted for within HRTW formalism applied up to 12.0 MeV incident neutrons. Compound nucleus and direct cross sections were added incoherently. Gilbert-Cameron model for level-density has been adopted for all nuclei involved in this evaluation. The parameters were fitted to reproduce the asymptotic behavior of discrete levels, as well as to correctly describe the observed cross sections. Complete g-ray cascades for every excited nucleus were calculated using M1, E1 and E2 electromagnetic transitions. g-strength functions for E1 transitions from the RIPL3 MLO1 formulation by Pluyko. Occasionally, we resorted to energy-dependent parameter scaling or tuning factors, available in the EMPIRE code, to account for model deficiencies. These corrections were typically on the level of 1-2% or less and can be found in the input files. Whenever possible the reaction model parameters used in the 57Fe evaluation were kept consistent with those used in the 56Fe evaluation.
FAST NEUTRON RANGE ------------------ MF=3 Neutron cross sections EMPIRE calculations adjusted to reproduce experimental data were adopted unless stated differently below.
MT=1 Total The fluctuations provided in the ENDF/B-VII.1 were derived from the abundance-weighted 56Fe(n,total) cross section. To restore the fluctuations, we performed a generalized least-square linear spline fit to the data of Harvey [5] and that of Pandey [6] in the region from 190 keV to 8 MeV. Both sets were in excellent agreement, differing only slightly in their treatment of the neutron time-of-flight. At the energy resolution of our spline fit, this difference was not observable. The fluctuations were distributed to the 57Fe(n,elas) and 57Fe(n,g) cross sections such that both the energy average elastic and capture cross sections were preserved and so that they sum to the fluctuating total cross section. The data of Hibden et al. [7] were disregarded as the target was an isotopically-enriched iron oxide target and the target composition was not given to enough precision to extract meaningful data.
MT=2 Elastic scattering This evaluation is distinctly different from ENDF/B-VII.1 Apart from the lower thermal region, the new evaluation adopts smooth EMPIRE calculations above the resonance region, contrary to ENDF/B-VII.1 which propagated 56Fe fluctuations up to several MeV.
MT=4, 51-91 Inelastic scattering 57Fe is a special case since the inelastic threshold lies inside the resonance region requiring the Reich-Moore formalism and the ENDF-6 option LRF=7, as described in the resonance section.
MT=5 (n,anything) Sum of all reactions not given explicitly in another MT number as calculated by the EMPIRE code. This MT includes majority of the reaction channels - namely all those for which we do not provide a complete set of exclusive emission spectra. The reason for this unusual representation is a difficulty to disentangle contributions of different reactions to the gamma spectrum from the final residue. This becomes an issue at higher incident energies when multiple reactions contribute to the production of a given residue. Note that exclusive gamma emission spectrum is required by the ENDF-6 format for each reaction that is treated as exclusive. In the MT=5 representation, the cross sections can be obtained by multiplying cumulative cross section given in MT=5 by the relative yields for production of the residual nuclei given in the subsections of MF/MT=6/5. Particle and gamma emission spectra are summed up over the MT=5 reactions into the inclusive spectra given in the respective subsections of MF/

MT=17, 22, 28, 107, ...,849 EMPIRE calculations adjusted to reproduce experimental data. MTs NOT present! Included in MT=5.

EMPIRE CODE PARAMETRIZATION ---------------------------
Nuclear reaction model code EMPIRE-3.2.3 Malta (SVN rev. 4977; source rev. 4977) by M.W.Herman et al [8,9].
EMPIRE dimensions (dimension.h): NDNUC= 160 NDEXCLUS= 50 NDEX= 241 NDLW= 100 LEVCC= 40 NDLV= 40 NDBR= 40 NDMSCS= 4
The following EMPIRE-code modules and features were used in the current evaluation: - Spherical and deformed Optical Model including coupled-channels code ECIS06 by J. Raynal - Soft-rotator deformed Optical Model including coupled-channels code OPTMAN by E.Soukhovitskii and coworkers - Hauser-Feshbach statistical model including width fluctuation correction, and the optical model for fission with partial damping - Exciton model with Iwamoto-Harada cluster emission and Kalbach systematic angular distr. (code PCROSS by R.Capote et al) - Complete gamma-ray cascade after emission of each particle, including realistic treatment of discrete transitions - Access to OM segment of the RIPL library [10] - Built-in input parameter files, such as masses, level density, discrete levels, and gamma strength functions based on the RIPL library [13] - Automatic retrieval of experimental data from the EXFOR library - ENDF-6 formatting (code EMPEND by A.Trkov) coupled to graphical presentation capabilities (code ZVView by V. Zerkin) through the chain of PrePro codes by D. Cullen - ENDF checking codes (CHECKR, FIZCON, PSYCHE)
EMPIRE options -------------- Following options and deviations from the default values of the parameters were employed in the EMPIRE calculations:
- CC calculations using soft-rotor omp for the incident channel. - CN decay and Direct cross sections added incoherently. - Traditional Hauser-Feschbach Tlj_{CC}(E)=Tlj_{GS}(E-Egs). - HRTW width fluctuation correction calculated up to 9.90 MeV. - Tlj coupling for the top CN bin up to incident 9.90 MeV. - CN anisotropy calculated using Blatt-Biedenharn coefficients. - Coupled Channels Method used for Tl calcul. in outgoing ch. - Discrete levels were taken from the RIPL-3+ library based on the 2015 version of ENSDF. - Gamma-transition multipolarity set to 2. - GDR parameters taken from RIPL/Exp.data+Plujko systematics. - E1 strength function set to RIPL MLO1 - Gilbert-Cameron (EMPIRE 2.18) level densities. - Preequilibrium mechanism treated in terms of the exciton model with the Iwamoto-Harada model for emission of clusters, and Kalbach systematics angular distributions (see RIPL-1)
